newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Netherlands backs SAfrica economic growth strategy.
newsitem.headline: Netherlands backs SAfrica economic growth strategy.

text.p: Dutch Economic Affairs Minister Hans Wijers on Friday backed South Africa's new macro-economic growth strategy and urged the country to press ahead with the privatisation of state assets.
He told a media conference that although union leaders had expressed reservations to him about the government's new economic strategy, "it sounds very logical and consistent... so let's go for it."
Wijers is leading a delegation of Dutch business leaders and officials to South Africa. The delegation coincides with the state visit by Queen Beatrix of the Netherlands.
The only way in which South Africa could attract the foreign capital it needed was to press ahead with its plans to privatise or "restructure" state assets such as Telkom, Wijers said.
"You need to do that because you will not achieve (the targeted) six percent growth if you do not bring in foreign capital," he said.
This, in turn, would require extensive deregulation and the introduction of a wide range of investment incentives.
Asked whether high levels of crime would not deter foreign investors, Wijers said it was no worse that in other countries and underscored the need to stimulate growth.

Crime, he said, was caused by "differences in wealth in this country" while the justice and police systems had to be restructured to turn their focus away from enforcing apartheid to "working to catch thieves".

Asked whether he was concerned about the future of South Africa after President Nelson Mandela retired, he said he had been impressed by the large range of talented and committed black politicians and businessmen he had met in South Africa.
"There is no reason whatsoever to be worried about that. There is a huge degree of commitment to the strategy that this country has to follow in the years to come."
Netherlands currently holds the chairmanship of the European Union and Wijers said he had been asked what support it could give South Africa in its negotiations on a free trade agreement with the EU.
"What I have said is that we will use our influence as much as possible to make this process as favourable as possible for South Africa," Wijers said.
But, to "manage expectations", he had warned that being chairman of the EU did not mean that the Netherlands could do what it wanted because of the many different interests at stake.
"But we will try to bring Europe to a situation where it puts its money where its mouth is," he said.
He said members of his delegation had held wide ranging talks with businesses in South Africa and there were "all kinds of projects in the pipeline" in various areas.
For example, agribusiness giant Cebeco-Handelsraad had signed a declaration of intent with FoodCorp to explore possible joint ventures.
He said his delegation was "much more positive about the opportunities here" after their visit.
